title: The name of the sword
hookLine: Tyag Mal, youngest son of Guru Hargobind, fights so bravely he is called Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword

cards: Some people get their names twice: once from their parents, and once from what they do. The kid everyone calls Doc because she bandaged the whole playground.
The grandfather everyone calls Captain, though he never captained anything but the family. The second name tells you who a person became. The child Guru said the next Guru was at Bakala.
To find out who he meant, the story goes back about thirty years, to Guru Hargobind's household and his youngest son, a quiet boy who got his second name on a battlefield.
A name that means a sword, given to a man who would then spend twenty years in quiet.

teach.b: He was born in Amritsar in 1621, and his parents named him Tyag Mal. Tyag means renunciation, letting go. Tradition remembers him as thoughtful, inward, drawn to quiet.
Then came the battles of Guru Hargobind's later years, the ones from day sixty-eight.
At the battle of Kartarpur, in 1635, the boy was about thirteen or fourteen.

teach.h: TEGH BAHADUR — BRAVE OF THE SWORD.
teach.b: Tradition says he fought with such courage and skill with the sword that his father gave him a new name: Tegh Bahadur. Tegh is a sword. Bahadur means brave.
Brave of the sword. You might expect a boy with that name to become a great commander. He did the opposite.
After his father's death, he went with his mother, Mata Nanaki, and his wife, Mata Gujri, to Bakala, a village near the Beas where his mother's family lived.
There, for about twenty years, he lived very quietly.

Tradition says he spent long hours in meditation in a small room below ground, working with his hands and keeping to himself, while the Guruship passed to his nephew, Har Rai, and then to the child Har Krishan.
People who met the grown man found someone gentle and still, who wrote hymns of calm detachment, some of them now in the Guru Granth Sahib.
The boy they called brave of the sword spent those years in stillness at Bakala, making no claim. Tomorrow, someone comes to the village looking for him.

how: Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, as both brave and deeply contemplative; his hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, often about detachment and calm, are sung in gurdwaras and at Sikh funerals.

o: brave of the sword, a name won in battle
a Persian title for a Mughal governor
a sword handed down from the first Guru

games.q: what's inside the name — tap the pairs.
p: where he lived quietly for years

s: Tegh Bahadur was the name he was born with
he was born Tyag Mal; his father renamed him after the battle of Kartarpur.
after his bravery he became a great commander
he went to Bakala and lived quietly for about twenty years.
some of his hymns are in the Guru Granth Sahib
his hymns of calm detachment are part of the scripture.

games.q: you're a young man everyone now calls brave of the sword. your father has died. what do you do with the next twenty years?
o: raise an army of your own.
go to a quiet village and meditate.
go to the emperor's court to seek a post.
games.why: Tegh Bahadur went to Bakala with his mother and wife, and lived there quietly for about twenty years.

practice: Let one moment come back when you were braver than you expected: you spoke up, you stayed, you walked into a room you dreaded. It doesn't have to be dramatic; feel it again in your body.
Then notice how quiet that courage is now, sitting inside you, not needing to prove anything.

wordCard.voice: Tegh Bahadur. Brave of the sword, the name given to the boy Tyag Mal after he fought bravely at the battle of Kartarpur in 1635.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi, from Persian: tegh, sword; bahadur, brave.

carryVoice: Your line: brave, then quiet. A sword for a name, and a quiet room for twenty years. That's seventy-four.
